chapter: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington
title: The blank tape of the Ellington argument
summary: Ellington asked Willard to suppress the disc jockey's tape, which turned out to be blank.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: One of the things that you probably don't know -- I just told Bill Struther the other day, that you know he had come back to get an interview with Duke, and when you and Duke got into this he turned his tape recorder on, and I thought, 'Oh, great. He has a record of this, because I'd like to listen to this again.' After Duke had to go onstage for the next show --
What'd he do, erase it accidentally?
No. He said to me, he says, 'Patty,

I don't want that ever to be broadcast. What just went on in here," he said, "must never be broadcast." He said, "Get that tape." I said, "I can't get that tape from that man. That man has something that nobody has, what just went on in there." He says, "Your assignment is to get that tape. I don't want it broadcast." And so I went out looking for Bill Struther in the Grove, and he'd gone. He took his tape and went home. And so I figured that I'd wait until the next morning and try to figure out something, went home worrying about it. The first thing in the morning -- because Duke told me I was to deliver the tape to the hotel the next day -- the first thing in the morning I was trying to figure out what to say to Bill Struther, and the phone rang and it was Bill Struther, and he said, "The most horrible thing has happened. I couldn't wait to play that tape again this morning. I put it on, it's blank." I swore -- I told Duke --

I told him he did it, he did it. And he went, "Heh, heh, heh." But -- because Bill still cannot figure out -- he recorded lots of interviews, he was very familiar with the tape recorder, it never happened to him before or since, but that tape was blank.
Well, good. Because I'm sure people could have read a lot of things into it that weren't really there, because we weren't really angry at each other.
But he had a definite viewpoint and I had a definite viewpoint, and maybe your voices do raise, but there was no anger.
No, no. I don't remember anything at all about anger, but two very --
I just couldn't believe he was saying that, you know.

I couldn't either, and I think that's what bothered him, that nobody would want to hear him say that or believe that he really thought that emotion didn't go into music. I think it would have been an unpopular kind of a sentiment or a statement or a feeling for him.
Well, I'm glad the tape wasn't -- I'd like to have heard it, but it might have gotten into the wrong hands and been played -- some of it played out of context, and it could have been bad.
